title: Relationship check-in questions: how to do a weekly check-in with your partner
summary: Relationship check-in questions that actually get honest answers, plus a simple 20-minute way to run a weekly check-in with your partner.
body_markdown:
A weekly relationship check-in is a short, planned conversation where you and your partner ask each other a few of the same questions every week: what felt good, what felt off, and what you need from each other next. Fifteen or twenty minutes. That's it. The questions do most of the work, which is why they're worth choosing carefully.


Below is a set that works, grouped by what each one is for, plus a simple way to run the conversation so it stays something you both look forward to instead of something one of you quietly dreads.


## A simple shape for the twenty minutes


Check-ins that last tend to follow roughly the same order. Start warm, get honest in the middle, end on something small and concrete.


1. **Appreciation first.** Each of you names one specific thing the other did this week. Specific matters. "Thanks for everything" doesn't land the way "you dealt with the landlord so I didn't have to" does.
2. **How each of you is doing, separately.** Not the relationship yet. Work, sleep, stress, your mom. A lot of what feels like relationship tension is one person running on empty.
3. **The relationship itself.** What felt close, what felt off. This is where the harder questions go.
4. **One thing for next week.** A single small ask or plan. Then stop, even if it's going well.


Take turns answering. Whoever usually talks more goes second.


## Easy questions to open with


- What's one thing I did this week that you liked?
- When did you feel most like "us" this week?
- What are you looking forward to?
- Is there anything you're carrying right now that I don't know about?


## Questions about how you're each really doing


- How full is your tank right now, honestly?
- What's taking up the most room in your head?
- Is there something I could take off your plate this week?
- Did you get enough time to yourself?


## Questions about the two of you


- Was there a moment this week you felt far away from me?
- Did I say or do anything that stuck with you in a bad way?
- Was there something you almost brought up and didn't?
- Have we had enough time together that wasn't about logistics?
- Is there anything we keep arguing about that we should actually sit down and solve?
- How's our physical closeness feeling to you lately?


You don't need all of these every week. Pick two or three and rotate. Some weeks the honest answer to every one is "no, we're good," and that's a completely successful check-in. Those quiet weeks are one of the[green flags in a relationship](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/green-flags-in-a-relationship) , not wasted time.


## Questions for looking ahead


- What's one thing you'd like more of next week?
- Is anything coming up that's going to be stressful, and how do we want to handle it?
- Is there something we haven't done in a while that you miss?


## The one question worth keeping every week


Here's a pattern we see over and over in Maia conversations. The issue someone finally brings in, the one that feels enormous now, almost always started as something small they noticed months earlier and decided wasn't worth a whole conversation. A comment at dinner. A weekend that went sideways. Not big enough to raise on a random Tuesday, so it never got raised. Then it got company.


That's why "Was there something you almost brought up and didn't?" earns a permanent spot. It gives the small thing a door to come through while it's still small. And when your partner answers it honestly, thank them, even if what they say stings a bit. How you react this week decides whether they answer honestly next week.


## How to keep it from turning into a trial


The fastest way to kill a check-in is to make it the place where the week's complaints get delivered in bulk. If your partner learns that Sunday is when they get handed the list, they'll start being busy on Sundays.


- **Talk about your experience, not their character.** "I felt kind of alone Wednesday night" opens a conversation. "You're always on your phone" closes one.
- **If something gets heated, park it.** Agree on a time to come back to it. The check-in is for noticing things, not solving everything in twenty minutes.
- **Don't save it all for check-in day.** This works alongside saying things in the moment, never instead of it.
- **Keep the time limit, even on good weeks.** Ending while it still feels easy is what makes the next one easy to start.


If every honest answer seems to slide into[the same argument you always have](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/we-keep-having-the-same-argument) , that's useful information, not proof the check-in failed. It means there's one conversation that needs its own time, outside the ritual.


## Making it stick past week three


Most couples don't stop because the check-ins go badly. They stop because nobody puts the next one on the calendar. Attach it to something you already do: Sunday coffee, the walk after dinner, the drive home from the grocery store. Keep the questions you like in a note on your phone so nobody has to invent them on the spot. Miss a week? Pick it back up. Nothing is ruined.


It helps to know what you're protecting, too. Couples who[turn into a logistics team](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/weve-become-a-logistics-team-not-a-couple) rarely notice it happening. A weekly check-in is one of the few habits that notices for you. And once the ritual is in place, a neutral outside read can catch the patterns neither of you can see from the inside, which is what[AI check-ins](https://www.ourmaia.com/post/ai-check-ins-to-keep-your-relationship-healthy) are built for.


If you're not sure which questions fit where your relationship is right now, or there's something you keep almost bringing up and can't find the words for, you can talk it through with Maia first, on your own or together. Sometimes the best check-in starts with getting clear on what you actually want to say.
